title: Pick an environment you can actually keep
objective: By the end of this lesson you have a Unix-like environment on the machine you own, and you can say what you gave up to get it.

blocks.text: Every other course in this track assumes a Unix-like shell: a window where you type a command and it runs. Windows does not give you one by default, macOS does, and Linux is one. This lesson gets you to a working shell and tells you honestly what each route costs, because the cheapest route to start is not always the one you can keep.

rows: WSL 2 — a real Linux kernel inside Windows
A one-time install and a reboot. Files are in two worlds at once, which confuses people for the first week
The Terminal app you already have
Nothing to install for the shell. But macOS is not Linux: some commands take different flags, and this track flags those where they matter
A locked-down machine you cannot install on
A browser shell from a cloud provider
Sessions reset, so anything you did not save is gone. Fine for a lesson, painful for a course
A machine you can install on but do not want to change
One install, then a clean Linux you can throw away. You must learn one extra command before you learn anything else

blocks.title: The cloud shell trade-off is real, and people discover it late
blocks.text: A free browser shell is genuinely the fastest way to run your first command. But most reset after a period of inactivity, and several keep only your home directory — so the compiler you installed in lesson three is gone by lesson five, and you will not know why. If you pick this route, expect to re-install tools, and keep your work in a git repository from the start.

blocks.caption: One command in PowerShell, run as Administrator
lines: wsl --install
# then reboot, and Windows will finish the setup and ask you to
# choose a username and password for the Linux side
# after the reboot, open the app called "Ubuntu" from the Start menu
/* This gives you a real Linux kernel, not an emulator. The Linux side has its
own filesystem; your Windows files appear under /mnt/c. Work inside the Linux
home directory (~), not under /mnt/c — file access across the boundary is
much slower and permissions behave differently. */

blocks.text: macOS: you already have a shell

blocks.caption: Open it and check
lines: Press Command-Space, type Terminal, press Return.
$ uname -s
Darwin
/* Darwin is the name of the macOS kernel. You have a Unix shell. What you do
not yet have is a compiler — that is the next lesson but one. */

blocks.title: What is a terminal, actually?
blocks.forWhom: for readers who have never opened one

blocks.text: A terminal is a window that shows you a prompt and waits. You type the name of a program, press Return, and the program runs and prints whatever it wants to say. That is the whole idea. It is not a special mode of your computer and it cannot break anything by being open.

The prompt is the text sitting to the left of where you type. It usually tells you who you are and where you are, and it ends in a symbol — often $ or %. When you see a command written as "$ uname -s" in these courses, the $ is the prompt, not something you type. Type only what comes after it.

blocks.caption: What you see and what you type
lines: teerakanok@laptop ~ %  uname -s
the prompt (given)     what you type

blocks.text: Linux, or a container on any machine

blocks.caption: If you want a clean Linux you can throw away
lines: # install Docker Desktop (macOS, Windows) or docker.io (Linux), then:
$ docker run --rm -it debian:12-slim bash
root@a1b2c3:/#
# you are now root inside a fresh Debian. --rm means it is deleted when
# you exit, so nothing you do here can touch your real machine.
/* This route is worth knowing even if it is not your main one: several
exercises later in this track need root or a second user account, and a
throwaway container is the safe way to have both. */

blocks.title: Get to a prompt and prove it
steps: Follow the route for your machine until you have a prompt
Run: uname -s     — expect Linux, or Darwin on macOS
Run: whoami       — this is the account you are running as
Run: pwd          — this is the directory you are in right now
Write down all three answers; the next lesson uses them
If any command printed "command not found", you are probably in PowerShell or Command Prompt rather than a Unix shell — check that you opened the right app
Run: echo $SHELL  — bash and zsh both work for everything in this track
blocks.expected: Three answers and a prompt you can get back to tomorrow. That last part is the real test: if your route was a browser shell, open it again in an hour and check whether pwd still shows the same directory and your files are still there. Finding that out now costs a minute; finding it out in lesson twelve costs an evening.

cheatsheet: Windows: wsl --install in PowerShell as Administrator, then reboot
macOS: Terminal is already installed; uname -s prints Darwin
Linux: you already have a shell
Cloud browser shells reset — expect to reinstall tools and keep work in git
docker run --rm -it debian:12-slim bash gives a throwaway Linux with root
In WSL, work in ~ and not under /mnt/c: slower, and permissions differ
The $ or % in a printed command is the prompt — do not type it
uname -s, whoami and pwd answer: what system, who am I, where am I

checkpoint.prompt: You are on Windows and want a Unix-like shell for this track. What does wsl --install give you?

choices.A: An emulator that translates Linux commands into Windows ones
choices.B: A remote Linux machine you connect to over the internet
choices.C: A real Linux kernel running inside Windows, with its own filesystem
choices.D: A theme that makes Command Prompt look like Linux

checkpoint.explanation: WSL 2 runs an actual Linux kernel. Your Windows files appear under /mnt/c, but work inside the Linux home directory: crossing the boundary is slower and permissions behave differently.

checkpoint.prompt: A printed command reads "$ uname -s". What do you type?
checkpoint.explanation: The $ is the prompt the shell prints for you. Typing it back gives "command not found: $".

checkpoint.prompt: Why does this lesson warn about free browser-based cloud shells?

choices.C: Many reset after inactivity and keep only your home directory
choices.D: They are slower than a local machine

checkpoint.explanation: Tools you installed disappear later in the course They are the fastest way to run a first command and a poor way to keep a course's worth of state. If you use one, expect to reinstall and keep your work in git.

checkpoint.prompt: Which route gives you root and a second user account safely, for the exercises later in this track that need them?

choices.C: A throwaway Docker container started with --rm

checkpoint.explanation: --rm deletes the container when you exit, so creating users and changing ownership inside it cannot affect your real machine.
